items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: The pop performers that they preferred were people that they had seen in movies like Frank Sinatra and Doris Day.

ctx.x: Did you personally have — I don’t want to say a problem — how did you adjust in your thinking and listening to the bop movement?

Oh that was a kind of an interesting thing because I was already aware of what was beginning to happen before the war. You see I got drafted straight off the campus, I was inducted about two or three months after I graduated from Yale. The first inkling was in the form of Dizzy Gillespie’s playing. And I first heard Dizzy in I guess it was 1938 because I remember discussing it with Marshall Stearns. His records came out and there were solos of Dizzy’s on various releases, including of course the Cab Calloway…

items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: They had to be songs that were sung by people like Frank Sinatra, Doris Day, and instrumentalists like Percy Faith and André Kostelanetz.

ctx.x: Bob Eberle. That was the equivalent of the way kids respond to rock music, you see. You notice these are practically all white bands. The Jimmie Lunceford band was not all that popular. The Basie band was more popular than Lunceford, but even Basie, I think, as far as the public was concerned, was way behind these other bands, Larry Clinton and so on and so on. They’re the ones that got the air play and the attention from the young fans.

So at all times, people like myself and Jerry King and the older Marshall Stearns, we were kind of strange outsiders, you might say, in our taste, because we were not in the mainstream of what the American public was listening to in the better grade of popular music. The singers were popular, but not as much as they became later. Except for Bing Crosby and, before him, Russ Colombo, who was, like Crosby, a radio phenomenon, they became popular through bands.
